children: Johnson & Johnson beat third-quarter earnings expectations and raised its full-year outlook on Tuesday, though stumbles in its medical technology business left investors lukewarm.
The healthcare giant posted third-quarter adjusted earnings of $2.59 a share, ahead of Wall Street's call for $2.52. Sales grew 5.9% to $25.4 billion to meet analysts' forecasts.

Management hiked its guidance on the back of the latest quarter, citing "strong operational performance." J&J is now targeting adjusted earnings in the range of $11.05 to $11.15 a share, up from a prior view of $10.96 to $11.11 in late July.

The updated range reflects the acquisition in July of Firefly Bio, a strategic collaboration with Sail Biomedicines, and a one-time charge for the proposed resolution of outstanding talc lawsuits. J&J also raised the low end of its annual sales forecast to bring the midpoint of the range to $101.2 billion, up from $101.1 billion.
Still, shares fell 2.6% to $256.87 in premarket trading Tuesday, lagging behind S&P 500 futures, which traded slightly lower.

The reaction might have something to do with J&J's mixed performance across its two core business units. Prescription drugs fueled strength in the latest quarter as sales rose 7.7% in J&J's pharmaceutical arm, compared to just a 2.5% increase in its medical technology division.

Highlights included 68% sales growth for Tremfya, which is positioned to succeed J&J's blockbuster autoimmune drug Stelara as its key patents continue to expire. Sales for antipsychotic medication Caplyta surged 66%, boosted by rising prescriptions for expanded uses including add-on depression therapy.

The company's MedTech division raked in $8.64 billion for the quarter, missing Wall Street's target of $8.74 billion as all four segments — cardiovascular, orthopedics, surgery, and vision — underperformed. Global surgery sales slipped 0.6%, while growth across the remaining three areas ranged from 3% to 4.5%.

J&J asserted that it was "taking focused action to improve results" in the MedTech business, adding that it remains confident in its long-term trajectory. The company reiterated it has a "clear line of sight to double-digit growth by the end of the decade," echoing commentary from Chief Financial Officer Joe Wolk earlier this year.

The company indicated Tuesday that it was weighing a spinoff of its orthopedics business. Multiple outlets reported earlier this year that Apollo Global Management was in talks to buy the business for roughly $20 billion.

Given its vast reach across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and biologics, J&J serves as a barometer for the broader healthcare sector. As the first big name to report earnings this quarter, J&J sets the stage for upcoming results from Novartis, Merck, and AbbVie later this month.
